title: Kirchhoff's Current Law: Why a Node Adds to Zero
topic: Kirchhoff's current law — at every node, the sum of currents flowing in equals the sum of currents flowing out; this is charge conservation, since the node has no capacity to store charge

beats.narration: Three wires meet at a single point — where does all the charge go?

elements.content: Manimo enters centre-screen
Three wires meet — where does the charge go?

beats.narration: Here's a node: one wire bringing five amps in, two wires carrying current out — three amps one way, two the other.

elements.content: T-junction: vertical wire from top, horizontal wire splitting left and right
Node dot at the junction
Arrow on the top wire pointing down (I_1 in)
Arrow on the right wire pointing right (I_2 out)
Arrow on the left wire pointing left (I_3 out)
I_1 = 5 A label on the top branch
I_2 = 3 A label on the right branch
I_3 = 2 A label on the left branch
one arriving, two leaving

beats.narration: Watch the charge dots stream in from the top. Five dots arrive every second. Three peel off to the right, two go left. Nothing piles up.

elements.content: Charge dots flowing along the inflow wire
Charge dots peeling off into the right outflow
Charge dots peeling off into the left outflow
Live count box: 'IN 5 A' top right
Live count box: 'OUT 5 A' bottom right
Balance readout: '∑ in − ∑ out = 0'
the node has no room to store charge

beats.narration: Sum of currents in equals sum of currents out, at every node. Five equals three plus two. That's Kirchhoff's current law.

elements.content: ∑ I_in = ∑ I_out
at every node
charge in equals charge out — no piling up, no leaking away

beats.narration: It's just charge conservation: a node is a wire, not a bucket — what arrives must leave.

elements.content: A node is a wire, not a bucket.
the foundation of nodal analysis
